papers.partial_detail: Read abstract, introduction (1.1-1.4), Theorem 3.1 and its use in the NP-completeness proof, Section 11.1-11.3, 11.8, Section 12 and Algorithm 1. Section 4-10 constructions and appendices not read line by line (about 3,100 text lines in total).
papers.what_it_is: A QCi arXiv preprint (Oct 2026) that compiles Karp's 21 NP-complete problems into standard quadratic programs on the probability simplex, with proofs, and no experiments.
papers.why_not: Hardware-neutral formulation theory by QCi authors. The text never names Dirac-3 or Dirac-3S, and the paper states it reports no solver or hardware results.

assertions.value: For a graph matrix with diagonal tau (0<tau<1), zeros on edges and ones on non-edges, the minimum over the simplex is tau divided by the clique number, and its strict local minimizers are the uniform distributions on maximal cliques. Stated as Theorem 3.1; the paper calls it a minimization-form restatement of the regularized Motzkin-Straus theorem, not a new result.
quotes: Its strict local minimizers are precisely the uniform distributions on maximal cliques, and its global minimizers encode maximum cliques.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem with proof in the paper; the proof was not checked here and the result restates known regularized Motzkin-Straus work.

assertions.value: The paper gives explicit simplex quadratic formulations for all 21 Karp problems: twelve by direct graph formulation and nine by factor-state formulation (six of those through binary-linear feasibility).
quotes: The catalog covers Karp’s 21 problems: twelve use direct graph formulations, and nine use factor-state formulations, including six obtained through binary-linear feasibility.
assertions.certainty_reason: Construction claim by the authors; individual constructions not verified here.

assertions.value: The paper reports no solver-performance experiments, basin measurements or hardware benchmarks, and says an exact formulation does not guarantee a large physical energy gap, robust analog behavior or quantum advantage.
quotes: It does not report solverperformance experiments, basin measurements, or hardware benchmarks.
Nor does a compact coefficient alphabet guarantee a large physical energy gap, robust analog behavior, or quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit directly in their own text.

papers.what_it_is: A January 2025 critical opinion article by Marin Ivezic on postquantum.com assessing QCi's Entropy Quantum Computing approach and Dirac machines.

assertions.value: The article's author states that as of 2025 no independent experiment has verified a performance advantage of QCi's EQC over best-in-class classical algorithms. This is an opinion article, not a survey of the literature.
assertions.anchor: Section: Is QCI's Noise-Harnessing Strategy Valid?
quotes: As of 2025, no independent experiment has verified a performance advantage of QCI’s EQC over best-in-class classical algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single commentator's absence-of-evidence statement dated Jan 2025; later work (for example 2026 QCi preprints) is not covered.

assertions.value: The author says QCi's advertised Dirac-3 counts (over 11,000 binary variables) are effective dimensionality of a photonic analog state space, not entangled qubits in the gate-computing sense.
quotes: These numbers refer to the effective dimensionality of the optical state space; however, it’s important to note these are not 11,000 entangled qubits in the gate-computing sense
assertions.certainty_reason: Interpretation by a third-party commentator; consistent with QCi's own description of variable counts but not independently measured.

assertions.value: The author's view is that EQC is best understood today as an analog photonic heuristic rather than a demonstrated quantum computer. Opinion.
quotes: EQC is best understood today as an interesting analog photonic heuristic rather than a demonstrated quantum computer.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the author as personal opinion, with no new measurements.

papers.partial_detail: The PDF is a 6-page browser print of a Photonic Integrated Circuits Magazine article (16 Mar 2026) with no text layer (images only). pdftotext returns nothing, so the quotes come from a Windows OCR transcript saved at quote_file_default; OCR has dropped letters in places (for example 'ocal', 'on y'). Quotes were chosen from clean lines only. A checker that uses pdftotext will find no text in the PDF.
papers.what_it_is: A QCi-authored trade-magazine article (Robinson, Nguyen, Dianat, Sua) summarizing Dirac-3 entropy computing benchmarks, citing Nguyen et al., Communications Physics 8, 411 (2025).

assertions.value: QCi reports that on a 30-node unweighted graph cut into 2, 3 and 4 subsets, Dirac-3 outperformed semidefinite programming (SDP). No numbers are given in the text; results appear only as histogram figures.
assertions.anchor: Article body, max-cut paragraph and figure
quotes: A 30-node unweighted graph was considered, which was then cut into a varying number of subsets.
Dirac-3 was able to outperform Semi-Definite Programming (SDP), a standard current way of solving the problem, for two, three, and four cuts
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor-authored summary of a small 30-node instance with no stated margins, run counts or time to solution.

assertions.value: QCi reports that Dirac-3 converged to a solution nearly 80% of the time on a 50-variable non-convex quadratic problem on which conventional gradient descent often got stuck in a local minimum. The article does not say what counts as a solution.
quotes: is able to converge to a solution nearly 80% of the time
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor-authored, one problem size, no classical convergence rate given for comparison.

assertions.value: QCi describes the current Dirac-3 as a hybrid photonic-electronic system and says an all-optical implementation is possible, not built.
quotes: While the current incarnation is a hybrid photonic electronic system, an all-optical implementation of the system is possible.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor statement about its own architecture; the possibility of all-optical operation is unproven.

papers.what_it_is: QCi resource-library index page for the eqc-direct software package, version 2.0.2; it holds a table of contents (Getting Started, Basic Usage, Advanced Usage, Dependencies, eqc_direct.client) and no technical content.

assertions.value: QCi publishes an eqc-direct software package, shown at version 2.0.2 on this page, with a single documented module eqc_direct.client. The page gives no description of what the package does.
quotes: eqc-direct software package - v2.0.2 - Quantum Computing Inc
assertions.certainty_reason: The page is a bare table of contents; only the existence and version of the package are shown.

papers.partial_detail: Read the full PyPI JSON description (README text, saved as eqc-models-pypi-description.txt); listed all 70+ .py modules in the wheel in memory; read the first 3,500 characters of the solvers, base and __init__ modules (saved as eqc-models-docstrings.txt), including the eqcdirect.py and qciclient.py solver headers. The .tar.gz was not opened. The rest of the wheel modules were listed only.
papers.what_it_is: QCi's eqc-models 0.21.0 Python package: model classes (QUBO, polynomial up to fifth order, portfolio, max-cut, QSVM, QBoost) and solver classes that submit to Dirac-1 and Dirac-3 through the qci-client cloud service or eqc-direct.

assertions.value: eqc-models 0.21.0 provides separate cloud solver classes for Dirac-3 (continuous and integer models) reached through the Qatalyst cloud service, built on the qci-client package; the same hierarchy also reaches Dirac-1.
quotes: Both Dirac-1 and Dirac-3 can be accessed using these solvers. Specific classes exist for the devices.
A solver class for quasi-continuous models that accesses Dirac-3 via the Qatalyst cloud service
assertions.certainty_reason: Package documentation backed by the wheel listing, which includes solvers/qciclient.py and solvers/eqcdirect.py.

assertions.value: eqc-models documents a polynomial model base class that supports up to fifth-order terms, matching the fifth-order interaction limit QCi states for Dirac-3S.
quotes: a base class for all models that utilize a polynomial formulation (up to fifth order)
assertions.certainty_reason: Software documentation of the modeling layer; it does not itself show the device accepts fifth-order terms.

assertions.value: In the package's own example for the Dirac-3 solver, a summation constraint value R is a Dirac-3 requirement the user must supply when solving.
quotes: R is the summation constraint value for the Dirac-3 requirement
assertions.certainty_reason: Code comment in the vendor's README example; consistent with the Dirac-3S paper's sum-constraint description.

assertions.value: The eqc-models direct-solver module falls back to a stub that raises an error when eqc-direct cannot be imported, and says this is likely because the Python version is 3.11 or newer.
quotes: eqc-direct package not available, likely because Python version is 3.11+
assertions.certainty_reason: Error text in vendor code; the likelihood statement is a hint, not a tested compatibility matrix.

papers.what_it_is: QCi resource-library index page for the qci-client software package, version 5.0.0; a table of contents (Getting Started, Basic Usage, qci_client.auth, qci_client.optimization) with no technical content.

assertions.value: QCi publishes a qci-client software package, shown at version 5.0.0 on this page, with modules qci_client, qci_client.auth and qci_client.optimization. The page does not describe behavior.
quotes: qci-client software package - v5.0.0 - Quantum Computing Inc
assertions.certainty_reason: The page is a bare table of contents; only existence, version and module names are shown.

papers.what_it_is: A QCi website news article describing Entropy Quantum Computing in lay terms, with CTO William McGann quotes and a BMW sensor-placement example; it names Dirac 1, not Dirac-3.
papers.why_not: The article names Dirac 1 as the machine behind EQC and does not mention Dirac-3 or Dirac-3S, so its figures cannot be attributed to those devices.

assertions.value: QCi's team estimates the current limit of its EQC photonic approach is about 30,000 qubits (modes), which it says could expand. This is a vendor estimate, not a measured result.
quotes: The team estimates that the current limit is about 30,000 qubits, but that could expand as research progresses.
assertions.certainty_reason: Unsourced vendor estimate in a promotional article; elsewhere QCi lists far lower variable counts for its devices.

assertions.value: QCi says EQC solved a BMW sensor-placement problem (more than 500 constraints, 3,854 variables in the main test) in about six minutes, placing 15 sensors to cover about 97 percent of the vehicle. No classical baseline is given.
quotes: Even with those constraints, EQC only needed about six minutes to arrive at the optimal solution for sensor placement.
Tests of EQC for this problem included problems of size 1,023, 2,888 and 3,854 in terms of variable count.
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor narrative with no method, baseline, or optimality proof; the word optimal is unverified.

papers.what_it_is: A QCi application note applying QBoost on Dirac-3 to the Kaggle credit-card fraud dataset and comparing with XGBoost on a balanced sub-sample.

assertions.value: On a balanced sub-sample of about 3,000 transactions (80% train, 20% test), QBoost on Dirac-3 and XGBoost both scored accuracy 0.84 and AUC 0.87; QBoost had higher precision (0.96 vs 0.87) and lower recall (0.70 vs 0.78). QCi's own test; single split described, no confidence intervals.
quotes: We created a dataset by sub-sampling of the majority class. We randomly chose a balanced dataset consisting of about 3000 samples.
Model Accuracy Precision Recall F1 Score AUC QBoost 0.84 0.96 0.70 0.81 0.87 XGBoost 0.84 0.87 0.78 0.82 0.87
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured table in a vendor note; balanced sub-sample is not the true 0.172% fraud base rate and no error bars are given.

assertions.value: QCi asserts that QBoost on its Dirac machines gives superior speed and power consumption over classical approaches. The page reports no timing or power measurement to support it.
quotes: is a classification method that leverages quadratic optimization solvers (such as QCi’s Dirac machines) to obtain superior speed and power consumption over classical approaches.
assertions.certainty_reason: Marketing-style statement with no supporting measurement on the same page.

assertions.value: The Kaggle credit card fraud dataset used in the note has 284,807 transactions, of which 492 (about 0.172%) are fraudulent.
quotes: It is comprised of a total of 284,807 transactions, with 492 of them (approximately 0.172%) being fraudulent.
assertions.certainty_reason: Dataset description restated by QCi; matches the widely published dataset card but not re-verified here.

papers.partial_detail: Read the abstract, introduction, Sections 2-5 (formulation, Dirac-3S, classical solvers, results, discussion, limitations) and the start of the conclusion, about 43,000 of 52,900 characters; the rest of the conclusion, methods supplement and references were not read.
papers.what_it_is: A QCi arXiv preprint (30 Sep 2026) benchmarking Dirac-3S on 75 DIMACS max-clique graphs through the Motzkin-Straus quadratic program against Armijo-PGD and Hexaly.

assertions.value: In QCi's own benchmark, Dirac-3S returned a clique at least as large as both Armijo-PGD and Hexaly on 62 of 75 DIMACS graphs. The comparison covers the unregularized Motzkin-Straus quadratic program only, two classical baselines, and no specialized clique algorithms.
quotes: Altogether, Dirac-3S matches or exceeds both classical solvers on 62 of the 75 graphs, i.e., on more than four-fifths of the benchmark.
The comparison therefore assesses the tested solver configurations on a common formulation, rather than establishing their competitiveness against the strongest specialized maximum-clique algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured counts from a vendor-authored preprint with disclosed scope limits; one hardware run set, no independent replication.

assertions.value: Dirac-3S reached the best known clique size on 33 of 75 DIMACS graphs, the same as Armijo-PGD (33) and more than Hexaly (26); where Dirac-3S was the sole leader its lead was only 1 to 3 vertices. On 42 graphs it did not reach the best known value.
quotes: Dirac-3S reaches the best known value on 33 of the 75 graphs, Armijo-PGD on 33, and Hexaly on 26.
Where Dirac-3S is the sole leader, its lead is only 1-3 vertices.
assertions.certainty_reason: Counts stated in text and Figure 2; the 42-graph remainder is derived by subtraction from the stated 33 of 75.

assertions.value: QCi states the Dirac-3S platform currently supports up to 9980 independent variables under summation constraints, with the benchmark graphs reaching about 4000 vertices.
quotes: In its current implementation, the Dirac-3S platform supports up to 9980 independent variables under summation constraints
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor specification stated in a vendor preprint; not independently measured.

assertions.value: In Table 2 (C250.9), Dirac-3S reached the optimal clique of 44 while Armijo-PGD on a GPU found 42, but Dirac-3S took about 120 s for 100 samples against about 10 s for Armijo-PGD (GPU). Dirac-3S was thus slower by an order of magnitude on that instance.
quotes: We run Dirac-3S for 100 num_samples, and report total time to run those 100 samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Table layout is garbled in the text extraction, so the solver-to-time mapping is inferred from row order (Armijo-PGD, Dirac-3S, Hexaly).
